title: Color as a Key Factor in Creating Sustainable Living Spaces for Seniors
target_construct: Creating sustainable, senior-friendly living spaces by optimizing color perception, color preferences, and visual comfort.

findings.antecedent: Monochromatic or monotonous interior color compositions
findings.consequent: Perceived as sad, depressing, unstimulating, uninspiring; not chosen by seniors

findings.antecedent: Interiors with strong tonal, saturation, or brightness contrasts
Compositions with colors from nature, earth, and natural materials (wood, wool, natural fabrics, leather, greenery)
Shades of blue, green, gray, and brown (natural world hues)
findings.consequent: Most liked/preferred by seniors; calming impact, eyesight not tired
findings.validation_evidence: Survey results (blue chosen by 26 seniors as favorite color)

findings.consequent: Least liked/preferred by seniors among cool colors
Easier for seniors to distinguish, but less preferred than shades of blue and green
findings.validation_evidence: Survey results (only 2 chose yellow, 6 chose red)

findings.consequent: Closely aligned with Le Corbusier's palettes (natural earthy tones: gray, beige, brown, muted blues, greens, ochre, sienna, off-white, black)
findings.validation_evidence: Comparison of preferred palette with Le Corbusier's palettes

findings.consequent: Absent in preferred palettes; visual dynamism achieved through diverse materials, textures, lusters, reflections, and transparencies
findings.validation_evidence: Comparison of preferred palette with Le Corbusier's theory

findings.antecedent: Chromatic monotony and lack of color stimuli in interiors
findings.consequent: Difficult orientation for older users due to lack of visual cues
Lack of stimulation, excitement, challenge; leads to apathy, illness, weariness; inhibits 'reserve capacities'

findings.antecedent: Stronger contrasts (3.5% higher than for people aged 20-30)
findings.consequent: Positively impact vision, object recognition, clear figure-ground difference for older adults
May appear grayish/pale to aging eyes; difficult to distinguish
Most easily perceived, vitalizing, energizing, calming for seniors

findings.antecedent: Expressive, dynamic, contrasting patterns (especially on floors and stairs)
findings.consequent: Impaired spatial/depth perception, difficulty distinguishing objects/steps, increased fall risk
Increased glare sensitivity, reduced contrast perception, reflections, perceived slipperiness, fear of falling
Overstimulation of sensory perception in seniors

findings.antecedent: Natural materials and contact with nature
findings.consequent: Regenerate nervous system, reduce stress, add energy; provide tactile, olfactory, acoustic qualities; easily recognized/perceived

findings.antecedent: Wood colors (light beige to dark brown, brown with yellow/orange/red saturation)
findings.consequent: More easily recognized and distinguished by seniors

components.name: Avoid Chromatic Monotony
components.description: Design interiors to avoid monochromatic, monotonous color compositions to prevent feelings of sadness, depression, and lack of stimulation, and to improve orientation.
components.validation: Supported by literature review and survey results showing seniors do not prefer monotonous spaces.

components.name: Use Contrasting Colors for Safety Elements
components.description: Employ contrasting colors for elements of equipment that may pose a safety risk to seniors to enhance cognitive stimulation, orientation, and overall safety.
components.validation: Supported by literature review on contrast sensitivity and object recognition.

components.name: Implement Stronger Contrasts
components.description: Utilize stronger contrasts (approximately 3.5% higher than for younger adults) to positively impact vision, object recognition, and figure-ground differentiation for older adults.
components.validation: Supported by literature review on age-related vision changes.

components.name: Careful Selection of Cool Tones
components.description: Avoid blue-green or blue-grey combinations. If using cool tones (violet, blue, green), select more intense hues or pair them with complementary colors from the warm spectrum, as cool tones may appear grayish or pale to aging eyes.
components.validation: Supported by literature review on age-related color perception changes.

components.name: Prioritize Warm Colors and Wood
components.description: Incorporate warm colors and natural wood, as they are easily perceived by seniors and have vitalizing, energizing, and calming effects.
components.validation: Supported by literature review and survey results indicating preference for natural earthy tones.

components.name: Adapt Colors to Functional Areas
components.description: Adapt interior colors to specific functional areas to create appropriate atmospheres, enhance memory, and support spatial orientation. Use subdued tones for relaxation areas (e.g., bedrooms) and brighter, warm, saturated hues with contrasting accents for activity areas (e.g., living rooms).
components.validation: Supported by literature review on color psychology and spatial orientation.

components.name: Avoid Complex Patterns on Floors and Stairs
components.description: Do not use expressive, dynamic, or contrasting patterns on floors and stairs to prevent impaired spatial and depth perception, difficulty distinguishing objects/steps, and reduced fall risk.
components.validation: Supported by literature review on age-related spatial perception deficits.

components.name: Opt for Matte Finishes on Floors
components.description: Avoid shiny surfaces and use matte finishes on floors to prevent glare, reflections, and the perception of slipperiness, thereby reducing the fear of falling.
components.validation: Supported by literature review on glare sensitivity and fall prevention.

components.name: Create Harmonious Color Palettes
components.description: Design harmonious color palettes, avoiding an excess of colors that can lead to sensory overstimulation in seniors.
components.validation: Supported by literature review on sensory overstimulation and survey results showing preference for harmonious spaces.

components.name: Prioritize Nature-Inspired Colors
components.description: Utilize colors found in nature, earth tones, and natural materials (e.g., wood, wool, natural fabrics, leather, various shades of greenery) as they are highly preferred by seniors and associated with well-being.
components.validation: Supported by literature review on biophilia and strong preference in survey results.

components.name: Consider Soft Pastels for Cognitive Impairment
components.description: For individuals with Alzheimer's disease, recommend soft, pastel, subtly stimulating colors (e.g., dusty pink, apricot) that are not overly 'flashy' or contrasting.
components.validation: Supported by research findings on Alzheimer's patients' sensitivities.

components.name: Integrate Natural Materials and Nature Contact
components.description: Incorporate natural materials and design to facilitate contact with nature to regenerate the nervous system, reduce stress, add energy, and provide multisensory qualities.
components.validation: Supported by literature review on biophilic design and stress recovery.

components.name: Leverage Wood's Natural Hues
components.description: Utilize the natural colors of wood, ranging from light beige to dark brown, and brown with yellow, orange, and red saturation, as these hues are more easily recognized and distinguished by seniors.
components.validation: Supported by literature review on color perception and natural materials.

components.name: Achieve Dynamism through Material Diversity
components.description: Instead of relying on bold, saturated dynamic colors, achieve visual dynamism and spatial variability through a diverse array of materials, textures, lusters, reflections, and transparencies.
components.validation: Supported by survey results showing preferred palettes avoid dynamic colors but use material diversity.

psychometric_properties.validity: Guidelines are based on a comprehensive literature review of age-related physiological changes in vision and chromatic perception, supplemented by a survey of seniors' color preferences, and compared with established color theories (Le Corbusier).

recommended_use: These guidelines are intended for architects and interior designers to inform color selection and combinations in the design of sustainable living spaces for seniors, ensuring visual comfort, supporting independence, and enhancing overall well-being. They can also serve as reference points for students and academic instructors in architectural design schools.
limitations: Cultural differences in color perception and preferences were not considered, as the survey was conducted among culturally homogenous participants in Poland.
The ambiguity in existing guidelines for effective color use in interiors often discourages bold color choices among designers.
Future research should explore the use of color in the care of people with terminal illness or in palliative care, and investigate methods such as color therapy, light therapy, or art therapy.
The study primarily focuses on visual deficits, but other sensory limitations in older adults are also relevant.

paper_metadata.title: Color as a Key Factor in Creating Sustainable Living Spaces for Seniors
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Color as a Key Factor in Creating Sustainable Living Spaces for Seniors
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Color as a feature of interior spaces is a fundamental component of human interaction with the built environment. Therefore, planning the design concept of an interior space with attention to color choices is extremely important, especially when the users of a given space include individuals who require additional support and care, such as the elderly. The colors used in architecture and interiors play a crucial role in the well-being of older adults, influencing their spatial perception, behavior, and activity. With age, color perception changes due to the effects of the aging process on vision. Visual deficits lead to shifts in sensory perception, which can, in turn, affect the sense of well-being, often creating a heightened sense of uncertainty. These changes in color perception due to aging may impact the color preferences of older people within their living environments. To create supportive environments for seniors, it is necessary to investigate which colors are most easily recognized, which colors are easiest to distinguish, and which colors are preferred by older adults. Based on a review of the literature and research findings on age-related changes in chromatic and spatial perception, design recommendations and guidelines have been developed. To supplement this knowledge, a survey was conducted among seniors to gather insights on their color preferences. Observations and analyzes of the survey results point to strategies for color use and underscore the importance of color in designing sustainable living spaces for seniors.
